cues.text: First: your alarm bell was exactly right. A ladder leaning on a wall can't reach higher than its own length, so 5.8 m must be wrong.
Here is your triangle again, drawn to scale: the ground, the wall, and the ladder slanting between them.
Notice where the ladder sits: it is the side opposite the right angle, and it is the longest side.
a² + b² = c² is really a statement about squares. Build a square on the 3 m side: 3 by 3, that's 9 little squares.
Now a square on the ladder: 5 by 5, that's 25. It's the biggest square, because the ladder is the longest side.
And the square on the wall, whose side we don't know yet.
Here is the whole rule: the two smaller squares, put together, exactly fill the biggest one. The square on the longest side is the sum, never one of the parts.
So, wall square plus 9 equals 25. That leaves 25 minus 9, which is 16 for the wall.
16 little squares fit in a square 4 by 4. So the side of that square, the height on the wall, is 4 metres.
Check: 4 m is less than 5 m, so it makes sense. And 9 plus 16 really is 25.
Now your line. You added 5 squared and 3 squared, which treats the ladder as one of the short sides. That's why the answer came out longer than the ladder.
The ladder goes alone on the right side, as c. Then h squared is 25 minus 9, which is 16, and h is 4 metres.
